text.tspan: Using Physics Encoded Recurrent Convolutional
Neural Networks to Model Cirrus Clouds
Maddy Stephens & Dr. Adam Smith
University of Puget Sound
Introduction
With man-made climate change becoming an increasingly
large threat to day to day life, combatting it is becoming
necessary pursuit. Understanding how parts of our atmosphere
affect the climate is critical, which leads us to our goal of
modeling the formation of ice crystals in cirrus clouds using
a neural network.
Figure 1: Cirrus Clouds
The Objective
The end goal of this project is to successfully find a solution
to the set of partial differential equations (PDEs) shown in
figure 2, developed by Dr. Steven Neshyba.
Figure 2: Neshyba's PDEs governing ice growth
These equations govern ice growth in cirrus clouds. The ice
crystals consist of two layers: the quasi-liquid layer (QLL) and
the ice layer. The first equation governs the total thickness of
these and the second governs just the QLL. Normally, we would
solve through standard PDE solving techniques, but these
techniques don't apply or are too inefficient to realistically
utilize for climate modeling. This problem makes searching for
alternative solutions more appealing, which is where neural
networks come in.
Neural Networks
PINNs
Neural networks offer a potential solution to this problem,
but what is a neural network, actually? In short, a neural
network is a mathematical approximation of a human brain.
As shown in Figure 3 below, it is made up of nodes and edges.
Each node is takes the sum of all edges coming into it and
applies a non-linear transform on it, and each edge has a
weight. With enough nodes and the right weights, they can
output anything, including the solutions to Neshyba's PDEs.
Once you've found the right weights, or "trained" the network,
getting the thickness of either layer is as quick as a bunch of
addition and multiplication operations. To train a network, we
define a loss function, or a measure of how wrong the network
is.
Physics Informed Neural Networks, or PINNs, expand upon
the idea of neural networks by training them using expected
behaviour. When training regular neural networks, we have a
set of expected outputs and compare them to our observed
outputs for loss. PINNs replace this with physics residuals.
Since Neshyba's PDEs are equalities, if we take the derivatives
of each network and then subtract the right hand side of the
equations, we should expect to get zero if the network is
correct. The issue with this is that the more complicated the
expected solution is, the harder it is to train the network, and
it happens that Neshyba's PDEs are quite difficult to train
with. In theory, given enough time, a PINN should be able to
solve these equations, but in practice, it hasn't worked.
When a problem is too difficult for neural networks, one
method for trying to remedy this is to simplify the problem.
PerCNNs, or Physics Encoded Recurrent Convolutional
Neural Networks, do this by encoding parts of the equation
in the network's architecture, but that's not the only thing
that simplifies the problem. The "Recurrent" part of the name
refers to the fact that the network feeds back on itself, which
allows the network to only take positional input and repeating
until the desired time step. The disadvantage is that we need to
have discrete time steps. Similarly, the "Convolutional" part
refers to mathematical convolution, which, in short, introduces
discrete positional steps. In theory, all of this simplification
should aid in training. Unfortunately, this wasn't the case over
my time with the project. In the future, it's worth looking into
further simplifications. The most promising of these is trying
to model the derivative of each together in addition to the use
of the PerCNN architecture.
I'd like to thank Professor Adam Smith for his advising,
Professor Steven Neshyba for making this project possible and
for meeting with me throughout the summer to ensure my
understanding of the problem was adequate. I'd also like to
thank Branson Jones for his work on this project in the
summer of 2024 and for passing off and documenting his code
for me.
